newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia takes cautious stand on privatisation.
newsitem.headline: Serbia takes cautious stand on privatisation.

text.p: Serbia has rejected a programme of mass privatisation and instead was taking a more cautious approach to transforming ownership of its key industries, a senior government official said on Friday.

Privatisation has become a big political issue, since reports leaked last summer to the press said the government was preparing to privatise postal services, oil and power industry. The government, however, has remained silent.
In the meantime, the Industry Ministry was assigned to prepare a new draft on privatisation and submit it to the parliament this September.
But Serbia's Industry Minister Oskar Fodor said it was highly unlikely the draft would be discussed before the November 3 elections.

"In this draft we have not dealt with privatisation of big state monopolies. Instead we tried to find out what companies can enter the process that would eventually rid us of very specific third form of ownership -- the socially-owned capital," Fodor told Reuters in an interview.
"But whatever we do, there will be no mass or voucher privatisation. It is a deception, the citizens are being given worthless coupons," the minister said.
Fodor insisted Serbia will not make the same mistakes as other so-called transition economies in East Europe where "sweeping privatisation brought public finances to the verge of collapse."

The draft says privatisation is not compulsory. Companies must only evaluate their capital until July 4, 1997 and leave it to their "boards" -- gathering workers' representatives and other owners -- to decide whether to privatise.
But Fodor said he did not expect workers to opt for privatisation of the socially-owned capital because they would not have to fear of getting sacked if their company is unprofitable.

The draft says only employees would enjoy some bonuses and would be able to buy up to $15,000 (dinar equivalent) worth of shares. Others (domestic and local companies and individuals) can buy shares at their face value.
"But the market will decide the real value," Fodor said, adding that shares would be auctioned publicly.
No privatisation proceeds would be used for deficit financing of the state funds, he said.
The Ministry of Industry suggested that two thirds of privatisation proceeds should be reinvested in the same company, while the rest goes to financing structural changes.
But those two thirds to be reinvested are still a matter of dispute among experts. Some wonder if fresh capital input into loss-making companies was economically justified.
The state-owned Development Fund would assume charge in case the rightful owner of capital was not pin-pointed.
In that case, the Fund would buy out the state's share in a company. The other solution is reinvesting proceeds as credits.

Those credits would carry lower interest rates and longer maturity. Thus companies get fresh working capital to kick start production, the minister said. "We think this is a way of of enabling companies to enter restructuring," he said.
According to Fodor, privatisation can be successful only with foreign capital input. But the Serbian government would not allow foreign investors buy and close down companies.
"We would like to discourage that and use economic measures to prevent foreclosure and lay-offs," he said.

Privatisation has been almost completed in retail trade, catering and most parts of tourism over past six years, as well as some segments of transportation, production of spare parts, textiles, pharmaceuticals and food processing industries.
The whole banking system has been transformed and banks are now constitued as shareholding companies. Of 120 banks, 90 are private, he said.
Fodor said almost 50 percent of Serbia's gross domestic product was generated by the private sector. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
